query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In thin, as-deposited Fe–Mn–Ni–Ge–Si high-entropy ribbons, the magnitude of the low-field magnetocaloric entropy change (ΔS) and the size of the thermal/magnetic hysteresis are both governed by the volume-average diameter of L1₀-type ferromagnetic nanoclusters that precipitate inside the nominally hexagonal, chemically disordered matrix; enlarging these nanoclusters increases ΔS roughly linearly but also increases hysteresis because larger, more coherent cluster/matrix interfaces move through higher elastic and chemical energy barriers.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equiatomic FeₓMnᵧNi_zGe₁₋ₓ₋ᵧ₋_zSi₀.₁ (0.25≲x≲0.35, 0.3≲y≲0.4) ribbon produced by single-roller melt-spinning, ~20 µm thick, fully as-spun (no post-processing); initially a single-phase, supersaturated hexagonal solid solution containing ≈3–5 nm coherency-strained ordered embryos.
generation.intervention: Isochronal vacuum annealing for 15 min at 573 K, 623 K and 673 K to coarsen the ordered nanoclusters without changing global composition.
generation.conditions: Magnetocaloric cycling in a 0–1 T field at 295–350 K; heating/cooling rate 2 K min⁻¹; cluster coarsening <25 nm to avoid full bulk transformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Mean diameter and volume fraction of L1₀-type ferromagnetic nanoclusters (measurable by HRTEM, SAXS or anomalous X-ray scattering).
generation.mechanism: Coarsening increases the per-cluster magnetic moment and the lattice-parameter mismatch at the cluster/matrix interface, raising the magneto-elastic driving force for the first-order transformation. The larger free-energy change boosts ΔS, but the higher interfacial energy and elastic barrier widen the hysteresis loop.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-spun baseline: (i) After 573 K anneal (cluster size →≈8 nm) ΔSₘₐₓ rises from ~2 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ to ~3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 1 T while hysteresis (ΔT_hyst between heating and cooling peaks) grows from ≈5 K to ≈9 K. (ii) After 623 K anneal (cluster size →≈12 nm) ΔSₘₐₓ ≈4 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, hysteresis ≈15 K. (iii) After 673 K anneal clusters impinge, initiating near-complete first-order transformation: ΔSₘₐₓ saturates (≤4.5 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) while hysteresis jumps to ≥20 K and cycling losses dominate.
generation.baseline: As-spun ribbon: single broad, weak magnetocaloric peak (ΔSₘₐₓ ≈2 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 1 T, ΔT_hyst ≈5 K).
generation.boundary: Prediction should hold for 0.2 T ≤ µ₀H ≤ 2 T, 270 K ≤ T ≤ 380 K, and for alloys whose room-temperature structure is predominantly hexagonal with ≤10 % pre-existing ferromagnetic phase; outside these ranges other phases or spin-glass behavior may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Absolute ΔS values may vary ±25 % with exact composition; the assumed linear increase of ΔS with cluster diameter could saturate earlier if elastic accommodation is poor; nanocluster chemistry might deviate from ideal L1₀ order at higher temperatures, altering both magnitude and slope of trends.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare one melt-spun ribbon batch, section into four pieces: keep one as-spun, anneal the others 15 min at 573 K, 623 K, 673 K. Measure (a) cluster size distribution by TEM/SAXS, (b) field-dependent magnetization (5–350 K, 0–2 T), (c) ΔS(T) from isothermal M(H) curves, and (d) hysteresis width from heating–cooling ΔS peaks.
measurements: Mean cluster diameter and volume fraction
Thermal hysteresis width (ΔT between heating and cooling peaks)
Magnetic hysteresis loss (area of M–H loops at 300 K)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (i) ΔS does not increase monotonically with measured cluster diameter or (ii) hysteresis width fails to increase (within experimental error) with cluster diameter; observing either constant or oppositely trending behavior across the annealed series would refute the proposed causal link.
